title: Gemini 3.1 Flash TTS - Text-to-speech with prompt-based voice direction
description: Google released Gemini 3.1 Flash TTS, a text-to-speech model that can be directed using detailed prompts. The prompting guide is surprisingly extensive, allowing control over accent, pacing, dynamics, and style. Simon demonstrates with multiple regional accents (Brixton, Newcastle, Exeter) and vibe-coded a UI for testing.
author: Simon Willison

title: The Future of Everything is Lies: Meat shields and ML accountability
description: Kyle Kingsbury introduces the concept of 'meat shields' - people employed to be accountable for ML systems under their supervision. This includes internal reviewers (Meta's content moderators), external accountability (lawyers penalized for LLM lies), and formalized roles (Data Protection Officers). Companies may use third-party subcontractors as 'throw under the bus' options when systems misbehave.
author: Kyle Kingsbury (via Simon Willison)

title: Datasette replaces token-based CSRF with Sec-Fetch-Site header protection
description: Simon landed a PR in Datasette replacing traditional CSRF tokens with Sec-Fetch-Site header protection, inspired by Filippo Valsorda's research shipped in Go 1.25. This removes the need for csrftoken input fields in templates and eliminates the skip_csrf plugin hook. Claude Code did much of the work across 10 commits, closely guided by Simon.
author: Simon Willison

title: OpenAI launches GPT-5.4-Cyber for defensive cybersecurity
description: OpenAI announced GPT-5.4-Cyber, a variant of GPT-5.4 trained to be 'cyber-permissive' for defensive cybersecurity use cases. They also extended their Trusted Access for Cyber program (launched February) where users can verify identity via government ID for reduced friction access. Simon notes this appears to be OpenAI's answer to Claude Mythos.
author: Simon Willison

title: Cybersecurity Looks Like Proof of Work Now - token economics of security
description: Drew Breunig notes that the UK's AI Safety Institute evaluation of Claude Mythos shows that spending more tokens (money) leads to better security results. This creates an economic equation: to harden a system, you need to spend more tokens discovering exploits than attackers will spend exploiting them. This makes open source libraries more valuable since securing them can be shared across all users.
author: Drew Breunig (via Simon Willison)

title: Steve Yegge vs Google on AI adoption - 'John Deere of tech' debate
description: Steve Yegge claimed Google engineering has the same AI adoption footprint as John Deere tractor company - 20% agentic power users, 20% refusers, 60% using basic tools. Addy Osmani countered that over 40K Googlers use agentic coding weekly with custom tools. Demis Hassabis called the post 'absolute nonsense' and 'pure clickbait'. Highlights industry-wide AI adoption patterns and internal culture challenges.
author: Steve Yegge, Addy Osmani, Demis Hassabis (via Simon Willison)

title: Exploring the new Servo crate - embeddable browser engine for Rust
description: Simon investigated the Servo v0.1.0 crate, which packages the Servo browser engine as an embeddable library for Rust. Claude Code built a CLI tool called 'servo-shot' for taking screenshots of URLs. While compiling Servo to WebAssembly isn't feasible due to threads and SpiderMonkey dependencies, Claude built a playground for html5ever and markup5ever_rcdom WebAssembly builds.
author: Simon Willison

title: The peril of laziness lost - LLMs lack the virtue of laziness
description: Bryan Cantrill argues that LLMs inherently lack the virtue of laziness. Work costs nothing to an LLM, and they don't optimize for future time. Left unchecked, LLMs make systems larger, not better. This highlights how essential human laziness is - our finite time forces us to develop crisp abstractions because we don't want to waste time on clunky ones.
author: Bryan Cantrill (via Simon Willison)

title: Meta's Muse Spark - first model since Llama 4, hosted with interesting tools
description: Meta announced Muse Spark, their first model release since Llama 4 almost exactly a year ago. It's hosted (not open weights) with API currently in 'private preview to select users', but available on meta.ai. Simon provides detailed analysis of the model's capabilities, tools, and reasoning features.
author: Simon Willison

title: Anthropic's Project Glasswing - restricting Claude Mythos to security researchers
description: Simon argues that Anthropic's decision to restrict Claude Mythos to security researchers under Project Glasswing sounds necessary. He discusses the security implications, the debate around open sourcing powerful AI models, and references Thomas Ptacek and Nicholas Carlini's perspectives. The system card for Claude Mythos shows exceptional vulnerability identification capabilities.
author: Simon Willison

title: Z.ai's GLM-5.1: 754B parameter MIT-licensed model with impressive SVG generation
description: Chinese AI lab Z.ai released GLM-5.1, a 754B parameter, 1.51TB MIT-licensed model. When asked to generate an SVG of a pelican on a bicycle, it unexpectedly produced HTML with CSS animations. The SVG quality was excellent, and when Simon pointed out a broken animation, the model diagnosed the CSS transform issue and provided fixed HTML. Simon also got a 'NORTH VIRGINIA OPOSSUM ON AN E-SCOOTER' with detailed comments and animations.
author: Simon Willison

title: Google AI Edge Gallery - official app for Gemma 4 on iPhone
description: Google released Google AI Edge Gallery, an official iPhone app for running Gemma 4 models (E2B and E4B sizes) directly on device. The E2B model is a 2.54GB download that's fast and useful. The app includes image Q&A, audio transcription (up to 30s), and an 'agent skills' demo with eight interactive widgets demonstrating tool calling. This is the first time Simon has seen a local model vendor release an official iPhone app.
author: Simon Willison

title: Ask HN: What Are You Working On? (April 2026) - AI Coding Agent Ecosystem
description: Hacker News community shares 470+ projects, with massive AI coding agent presence. Notable projects include: coding agent that beats Claude Code on SWE-bench (8/15 vs 5/15) at half cost, AI that turns YouTube into tutoring sessions, AI-native CLI tools, critique tool for AI agent output, agent registries, and many vibe-coded applications. Shows vibrant ecosystem of developers leveraging AI agents for practical tooling.
author: Hacker News Community

title: Eight years of wanting, three months of building with AI - syntaqlite case study
description: Lalit Maganti's detailed essay on building syntaqlite, high-fidelity devtools for SQLite. After procrastinating for 8 years due to tedious 400+ grammar rules, Claude Code helped build the first prototype in 3 months. However, the vibe-coded prototype had architectural issues, and they eventually threw it away and rebuilt with more human decision-making. Key insight: AI is unhelpful when you don't know what you want, and design has no objectively checkable answer unlike implementation.
author: Lalit Maganti (via Simon Willison)
